MMToM-QA: Multimodal Theory of Mind Question Answering

A 600-question video-plus-text benchmark that requires fusing what a household agent's actions look like with what the scene actually contains to infer their beliefs and goals — humans score 93% on the multimodal condition, but GPT-4, GPT-4V, and every open text/video model sit near chance.

// the gap

What problem is this solving?

Theory of Mind (ToM) — inferring another agent's beliefs and goals from their behavior — is usually tested with one modality at a time. Text-based ToM QA benchmarks (FANToM, Sap et al.'s Social IQa, the classic Sally-Anne adaptations) give a model a written scenario and ask about a character's belief. Video-based benchmarks (AGENT, Baby Intuitions Benchmark, PHASE) show an agent moving through a scene and ask about its goal. Both traditions inherited a premise from classic developmental psychology experiments — that a single, fully observed data stream is enough to test ToM. The authors argue that's not how humans actually do it: a person forms beliefs about someone else's mind from whatever partial evidence is on hand, then flexibly fuses it — what you can literally see them do (video) plus facts you know about the world that the camera can't show you (e.g., what's actually inside a closed cabinet or fridge, which only the text description states). Neither modality alone gives a complete picture, and no prior benchmark tests whether a model can combine them.

The paper also identifies a second, subtler gap: existing text ToM benchmarks isolate belief inference and goal inference into separate questions, and lean almost entirely on short-term true/false-belief tests reminiscent of Sally-Anne. MMToM-QA's authors point out this misses two things real ToM reasoning requires: joint inference (a person's goal is often only decodable once you've inferred their belief, and vice versa), and long-horizon belief tracking (updating what you think someone believes as they take more actions over time, not just after one look). MMToM-QA is built specifically to force both modality fusion and this richer, jointly-conditioned belief/goal reasoning, using long, procedurally generated household-activity videos (134 videos, 1,462 frames and 36 actions each) rather than short synthetic clips or single-sentence vignettes.

// how it works

The method

Each of MMToM-QA's 600 questions pairs an RGB-D video clip of a person (simulated in the VirtualHome-Social household simulator) with a text description of the apartment's contents and the person's actions, then asks a binary-choice question about their current belief or goal — always with one option "significantly more likely" rather than certainly true, mirroring how humans reason under uncertainty. Questions split into two families, each with sub-types illustrated in Figure 2: belief inference (Type 1.1 true belief, 1.2 false belief, 1.3 long-term belief tracking — 300 questions total, 100 per type) and goal inference (Type 2.1 goal given true belief, 2.2 goal given false belief, 2.3 goal given updated belief, 2.4 goal given future actions — 300 questions, 75 per type). Figure 1 shows why fusion actually matters for a real item: the video shows a person passing a wine glass without taking it, then approaching either cabinets or a microwave; only the text reveals cabinets have no cupcake but the microwave does — a model has to combine both streams to conclude she's after the cupcake, not the wine glass.

Questions are generated procedurally, not hand-written: a household state and an action trajectory are synthesized in VirtualHome-Social, a question type and two competing hypotheses are sampled given that trajectory, and GPT-4 turns the ground-truth state/action/hypothesis triple into natural-language scene descriptions and the final question (Figure 9). Because ground truth comes from the simulator rather than crowd annotation, every question has a verifiably correct answer. Alongside the 600-question test set, the authors release 1,000 procedurally synthesized training videos with full state/goal/belief annotations, plus a separate 40-video, 120-question "human test set" built from 3 participants with no prior exposure to the system controlling an avatar via the human interface, used purely to check generalization beyond synthetic behavior.

The paper's second contribution is a baseline method, BIP-ALM (Bayesian Inverse Planning Accelerated by Language Models), built to actually exploit the multimodal setup rather than just prompt an LMM end-to-end. A visual perception module (adapting Blukis et al. 2022) turns video frames into symbolic scene graphs (e.g. In(apple, kitchen cabinet), Closed(fridge)); GPT-4 does the same for the text, parsing it into an initial state, an action sequence, and the two hypotheses implied by the question. These are fused into one symbolic state/action trace. BIP-ALM then treats the person as a POMDP-optimal planner and runs classic Bayesian inverse planning — computing which of the two hypothesized (goal, belief) pairs makes the observed action sequence more likely under Bayes' rule — but replaces the usual expensive forward-planning/RL step with a finetuned language model (GPT-J-6B or LLaMA-2-7B) that directly estimates the action-likelihood term from the symbolic state.

P(g1,bt1|s1:t,a1:t) / P(g2,bt2|s1:t,a1:t) = π(aᵗ|g₁,b₁ᵗ)·P(b₁ᵗ|b̂₁ᵗ⁻¹,sᵗ)·∏ π(aτ|g₁,b̂₁τ)π(aᵗ|g₂,b₂ᵗ)·P(b₂ᵗ|b̂₂ᵗ⁻¹,sᵗ)·∏ π(aτ|g₂,b̂₂τ) // the odds ratio BIP-ALM evaluates between the two answer hypotheses H1=⟨g1,b1⟩ and H2=⟨g2,b2⟩; π(a|g,b) — the action-likelihood policy — is the term a finetuned LM amortizes instead of running forward planning

The questions themselves are generated by a three-step pipeline (Figure 9): a planner drives the VirtualHome-Social simulator to synthesize a video and its ground-truth state/action trace; an "ideal observer" samples competing (goal, belief) hypotheses consistent with that trace at each timestep; and GPT-4 turns the sampled hypotheses, plus the ground-truth state and actions, into the natural-language scene description, action narration, and final two-option question. Because the hypotheses are sampled directly from the simulator's own ground truth rather than written by crowdworkers, every question is guaranteed to have a well-defined, verifiable correct answer.

// what they found

The results

The headline number is the human/model gap. On the full multimodal condition, human participants (N=180, tested on a random 20% sample of questions) average 93.0% accuracy. Every off-the-shelf multimodal model tested — InstructBLIP, Video-LLaMA 2, LLaVA, and GPT-4V — scores between roughly 40–46%, i.e. at or barely above the 50% chance line (Figure 4). Text-only, humans reach 82.5%; GPT-4 (zero-shot) reaches only 48.0%, and even after being wrapped in the two prompting techniques specifically designed to help LLM ToM — SimToM (52.5%) and SymbolicToM (63.0%) — GPT-4 still trails humans by 20–30 points. Video-only, humans drop to 68.9% (video alone is inherently harder for people too), while InstructBLIP, Video-LLaMA 2, LLaVA, and GPT-4V range from 42.2% (LLaVA) to 50.8% (InstructBLIP), again near chance.

The per-type breakdown (Table 1) is where the story sharpens: GPT-4(V) is not uniformly bad — it hits 94.0% (multimodal) and 97.0% (text) on Type 1.1 (true belief, short-term), essentially matching humans, because that question only requires reading off the true world state from the text. But on Type 1.2 (false belief, short-term) — the classic Sally-Anne test that most prior LLM-ToM papers target — GPT-4(V) collapses to 13.0% (multimodal) / 12.0% (text), i.e. worse than random, because it systematically conflates "what's true in the world" with "what the person believes." Goal inference is uniformly weak for GPT-4(V): its lowest score anywhere is Type 2.3 (goal given updated belief), 4.0% multimodal and 2.7% text-only, because the model assumes a person's goal must be among the objects in a container they just opened, missing that opening-then-closing-without-taking signals an updated belief that should shift the goal hypothesis to something unseen. Type 2.2 (goal given false belief) is comparatively better at 26.7% multimodal / 42.7% text, and the overall goal-inference average (All-goal) is 34.7% multimodal / 34.0% text.

BIP-ALM, by contrast, clears every baseline by a wide margin without ever seeing the questions during training: BIP-ALM w/ LLaMA-2 reaches 76.7% multimodal / 70.5% text / 61.2% video overall, and BIP-ALM w/ GPT-J reaches 75.3% / 71.7% / 59.7% — roughly 30 points above GPT-4(V) multimodal and competitive with (though still below) the human ceiling. The ablation (Table 3) shows finetuning the underlying LM on the 1,000-video training set matters (e.g. LLaMA-2 goal-inference accuracy jumps from 53.3% to 73.3% multimodal with finetuning), but even the un-finetuned BIP-ALM already beats GPT-4 alone, evidence the gain comes from the Bayesian-inverse-planning structure itself rather than just more parameters or more data. On the separate 40-video human-behavior generalization set (3 participants with no prior exposure to the system controlling the avatar, unseen apartments), BIP-ALM's advantage held up, indicating the structured approach transfers beyond purely synthetic training trajectories.

// does it hold up?

The eval read

The core empirical claim — a large, robust human/model gap on jointly fused belief-and-goal reasoning — is well supported: it replicates across three input conditions, seven question types, and eleven baselines, and the human numbers come from an actual controlled experiment (N=180, Prolific) rather than being asserted. The procedural generation is also a real strength for eval integrity: because every question's ground truth is derived directly from the VirtualHome-Social simulator state rather than human-written labels, there's no crowd-annotation noise floor to argue about, and the benchmark can't have been directly memorized during LLM pretraining the way a scraped or classic-literature-derived text benchmark could be (no model saw these exact synthetic apartments and avatars during training, since they're generated after any plausible pretraining cutoff and never publicly released as ground truth pairs prior to the paper).

That said, a few specific points temper how far the headline numbers generalize. First, the "video" input to LMMs is uniform frame sampling from long clips (up to ~4,000 frames per Figure 8's video-length histogram) — GPT-4V, LLaVA, etc. only ever see a handful of sparsely sampled stills, not the full temporal stream BIP-ALM's visual-perception module effectively processes via voxel maps and scene graphs across every frame. That's a legitimate difference in what "video-only" means for the two families of methods, and it inflates the apparent human-vs-LMM gap somewhat: an LMM given denser temporal input might do meaningfully better, so some of the video-only weakness is an artifact of how the LMMs were adapted rather than an inherent failure to do ToM from video. Second, BIP-ALM is not a fair apples-to-apples comparison with the zero-shot LLM/LMM baselines: its LM backbone is explicitly finetuned on 1,000 videos drawn from the same generative process (same simulator, same predicate vocabulary, same household object distribution) as the test set, while GPT-4/GPT-4V are evaluated purely zero-shot with no exposure to this domain. The 40-video "human test set" generalization check partially answers this (new apartments, real human actions), but it's a small held-out set from the same VirtualHome-Social pipeline and predicate schema, not an independent domain — it doesn't yet tell us whether BIP-ALM's symbolic-predicate approach would transfer to messier, real-world observation streams outside curated household simulators.

Third, the metric itself — binary forced-choice accuracy with chance at 50% — obscures the qualitative failure modes that the paper's own per-type analysis surfaces as the more interesting finding: GPT-4(V) isn't uniformly incompetent, it specifically cannot distinguish "what is true in the world" from "what the person believes" once those diverge (Type 1.2/2.2), a much sharper and more diagnostic claim than an aggregate 44–48% accuracy communicates on its own. A reader relying only on the topline bar chart (Figure 4) would miss that GPT-4V nearly matches humans on the easy true-belief type while being worse than random on the matched false-belief type — the aggregate number averages over a real capability cliff rather than describing uniform mediocrity.

baselines

Reasonably current for a January 2024 paper (GPT-4/GPT-4V, LLaVA, InstructBLIP, Video-LLaMA 2, plus the two contemporaneous LLM-ToM prompting methods SimToM and SymbolicToM), but the video input given to LMM baselines (sparse uniform frame sampling) is not equivalent to the dense, per-frame symbolic extraction BIP-ALM gets, so the video-only comparison somewhat favors BIP-ALM's design over the zero-shot LMMs' out-of-the-box video handling.

contamination

Low risk for the benchmark itself — questions and videos are procedurally synthesized from a simulator after any realistic LLM pretraining cutoff and were not previously public, so verbatim memorization is implausible. The bigger asymmetry is BIP-ALM's own finetuning on 1,000 videos from the identical generative distribution as the 600 test questions, which is closer to in-domain training than genuine zero-shot generalization, unlike the LLM/LMM baselines it's compared against.

what's missed

Aggregate accuracy hides the sharpest finding (GPT-4V near-human on true-belief, worse-than-chance on matched false-belief); the benchmark is also confined to a single scenario family (a person searching for household objects) and doesn't yet test desires, emotions, or multi-agent ToM, which the authors flag as future work.

would raise confidence

A version of the video-only condition that gives LMMs the same frame density/coverage as BIP-ALM's visual perception module, and a genuinely out-of-distribution generalization test (different simulator, different predicate schema, or real-world video) for BIP-ALM rather than just new apartments inside the same VirtualHome-Social pipeline.

// bottom line

The human/LMM gap is real and well-isolated by question type, and the procedural-generation design is a genuinely clean way to guarantee unambiguous ground truth without contamination risk — but the paper's own proposed fix (BIP-ALM) benefits from an in-domain finetuning advantage the zero-shot baselines don't get, so its numbers should be read as "a structured, trained approach beats zero-shot prompting on this task" rather than "we've closed the ToM gap for general-purpose models."

// takeaways

What to remember

  1. MMToM-QA is the first ToM benchmark to require genuine multimodal fusion — pairing long household-activity video with text describing world state a camera can't reveal — rather than testing video and text ToM in isolation like prior benchmarks (AGENT, FANToM, Social IQa).
  2. Humans hit 93.0% multimodal accuracy; GPT-4V, InstructBLIP, LLaVA, and Video-LLaMA 2 all land between 40–47%, at or below chance — and GPT-4(V)'s failures aren't uniform, they're concentrated specifically on distinguishing true world-state from a person's (possibly false) belief.
  3. The paper's own baseline, BIP-ALM, pairs classic Bayesian inverse planning with a finetuned LM standing in for the expensive policy-evaluation step, reaching 76.7% multimodal — but its finetuning on in-distribution synthetic data means the comparison to zero-shot GPT-4 isn't fully apples-to-apples.
